title: BasicMed & Unfamiliar Aircraft Risk

required_knowledge_points.title: BasicMed Qualification Requirements
required_knowledge_points.why: A pilot who transitions to BasicMed without meeting all four qualification criteria flies illegally — the most common mistake is not realizing the prior-medical-after-2006 requirement.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: To operate under BasicMed (14 CFR Part 68), a pilot must meet four criteria: (1) Hold a current and valid U.S. driver's license. (2) Have held a valid FAA medical certificate (any class) at any point after July 14, 2006 — that medical must not have been suspended, revoked, or withdrawn. (3) Complete a physical examination by a state-licensed physician (MD or DO) using the FAA Comprehensive Medical Examination Checklist (CMEC) — valid for 48 months to the day. (4) Complete an FAA-approved online medical education course (via AOPA or Mayo Clinic) — valid for 24 calendar months.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Four Qualification Criteria (14 CFR Part 68)
- **Hold a current, valid U.S. driver's license**
- **Previously held an FAA medical certificate** (any class) issued **after July 14, 2006** — and that medical was never suspended, revoked, or withdrawn
- **Physical exam by a state-licensed physician** (MD or DO) using the **FAA CMEC form** — valid for **48 months to the day** (not calendar months)
- **FAA-approved online medical education course** (via AOPA or Mayo Clinic) — valid for **24 calendar months**

### Common Failure Point
- Pilot's last FAA medical was issued **before July 14, 2006** → **not eligible** for BasicMed, regardless of current health
- The CMEC exam uses **48-month-to-the-day** expiration — missing one week makes you non-current

required_knowledge_points.title: BasicMed Operating Limitations
required_knowledge_points.why: A pilot operating under BasicMed who exceeds the altitude, weight, speed, or occupant limits is flying without valid medical authorization — an often misunderstood limitation.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: BasicMed operating limitations under 14 CFR 61.113(i): (1) Aircraft must have a maximum certificated takeoff weight of 6,000 lbs or less — removing seats from a heavier aircraft does NOT satisfy this requirement. (2) Maximum 6 occupants (pilot + 5 passengers). (3) Maximum altitude: 18,000 feet MSL. (4) Maximum speed: 250 knots IAS. (5) Flight must be within the United States unless the foreign country specifically authorizes BasicMed operations. (6) No compensation or hire. Exception: CFIs may instruct under BasicMed because they are paid for instruction, not for acting as PIC.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Aircraft Limits (14 CFR 61.113(i))
- Max certified takeoff weight: **≤ 6,000 lbs**
- Based on the **type certificate** — removing seats from a heavier aircraft **does NOT** satisfy this limit
- Max occupants: **6** (pilot + 5 passengers)

### Flight Envelope Limits
- Max altitude: **18,000 feet MSL**
- Max speed: **250 knots IAS**
- Must remain within the **United States** unless the foreign country specifically authorizes BasicMed

### Other Restrictions
- **No compensation or hire**
- **Exception:** CFIs may instruct under BasicMed — they are compensated for instruction, not for acting as PIC

required_knowledge_points.title: Unfamiliar Aircraft Risk & Negative Transfer
required_knowledge_points.why: A pilot rated for ASEL can legally fly any non-complex ASEL without further instruction — this regulatory gap is a known accident cause when pilots underestimate system differences.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: 14 CFR 61.31 allows a rated pilot to fly any aircraft within their rating category and class without additional training, unless a type rating, high-performance, or complex endorsement is required. The risk: negative transfer, where habits from one aircraft cause errors in another. Example: a Cessna pilot reaching for flaps in a Bonanza and accidentally retracting the landing gear. Fuel mismanagement is the leading accident cause in unfamiliar aircraft due to differences in tank selectors, fuel pumps, and gravity vs. pressure systems. AC 90-109A provides structured transition training guidance.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### The Regulatory Gap (14 CFR 61.31)
- A rated pilot can fly **any aircraft** within their **category and class** with no additional training required
- Additional endorsements required for: **Type rating**, **High-performance** (>200 HP), **Complex** (retractable gear + constant-speed prop + flaps)

### Negative Transfer — The Hidden Risk
- Deeply ingrained habits from one aircraft **cause errors** in another
- Classic example: Cessna pilot reaching right to retract **flaps** on landing rollout in a Bonanza — instead retracts the **landing gear**
- **Fuel mismanagement** is the #1 accident cause in unfamiliar aircraft
  - Different tank selectors (gravity vs. electric pump systems)
  - Low-wing aircraft require **electric boost pump** on takeoff and landing
  - Tab tanks, aux tanks, and tip tanks each behave differently

### Mitigation
- **AC 90-109A** recommends structured transition training
- Conduct first flights in unfamiliar aircraft as **test flights**: no passengers, no complex airspace

required_knowledge_points.title: Glass Cockpit Transition & Automation Surprise
required_knowledge_points.why: Transitioning to a glass cockpit without structured training is a documented cause of automation surprise and LOC-I — the leading cause of fatal GA accidents.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Glass cockpit / Technologically Advanced Aircraft (TAA) transition risk centers on automation surprise: the pilot does not know what mode the autopilot is in or what it will do next. Common failure: believing the autopilot is capturing an altitude when it is in a different mode. Information fixation on the PFD causes loss of outside visual reference. The FAA documents this in AC 90-109A, which recommends treating first flights in a new glass-cockpit aircraft as test flights: no passengers, no complex airspace, no high-density altitude. Programming a GPS on the runway is a leading distraction accident cause.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Automation Surprise — The Primary Risk
- Pilot does **not know what mode the autopilot is in** or what it will do next
- Common failure: assuming autopilot is **capturing an altitude** when it is in a different mode
- **Information fixation** on the PFD → loss of outside visual reference → Loss of Control In-flight (LOC-I)

### FAA Guidance (AC 90-109A)
- Treat first flights in a new glass-cockpit aircraft as **test flights**:
  - **No passengers**
  - **No complex airspace**
  - **No high-density altitude**
- Program the GPS **before taxiing** — runway programming is a documented distraction accident cause

### Autopilot Mode Awareness
- Know the difference between **HDG, NAV, APPR, VS, FLC** modes at all times
- Autopilot **does not protect against** spatial disorientation if the pilot does not monitor it actively
- Glass cockpits have **more failure modes** to learn, not fewer

lesson_overview:
## BasicMed & Unfamiliar Aircraft Risk

This lesson connects two things that seem unrelated at first — medical certification and aircraft transitions — but they share the same underlying theme: **a legal clearance is not the same as a safe clearance.** Being allowed to fly doesn't mean you're ready to fly. Understanding where that line is, in both contexts, is what separates a sharp private pilot from a statistic.

**BasicMed in depth.** You already know the four-step qualification criteria: a valid U.S. driver's license, a prior FAA medical issued after July 14, 2006 (and not revoked), a physical with a state-licensed physician using the CMEC every 48 months, and an online education course every 24 calendar months. But knowing the checklist is only half the fight. The nuances are where pilots get caught.

The prior-medical requirement trips people up most. If a pilot's last FAA medical was issued in 2003, they cannot use BasicMed — even if they're otherwise healthy and their driver's license is spotless. The cutoff date of **July 14, 2006** is non-negotiable. Similarly, the 48-month limit on the physician exam is calculated to the day — not to the end of the month like FAA medicals. Miss it by a week, and you're not BasicMed current.

The **operating limitations** under 14 CFR 61.113(i) are where BasicMed gets teeth. You're boxed into aircraft with 6,000 lbs max certified takeoff weight or less, 6 occupants maximum, 18,000 feet MSL ceiling, and 250 knots max airspeed. Those limits apply to the aircraft's *type certificate* — not to what's physically in the cabin. You cannot fly a Piper Navajo under BasicMed by removing two seats. The certificate says what it weighs and how many people it was designed to carry. One exception that surprises people: **CFIs may instruct under BasicMed** because their compensation is for instruction, not for acting as PIC of the aircraft.

**Unfamiliar aircraft: the regulatory gap.** Here's something that should make you pause. Under 14 CFR 61.31, a pilot rated for Airplane Single Engine Land can legally step into *any* non-complex, non-high-performance ASEL aircraft without additional training. That means a pilot who has only ever flown a Cessna 172 can legally hop into a Beechcraft Bonanza, a Piper Arrow, or a Grumman Tiger. No checkout required by the FARs.

This is a documented accident cause. The aerodynamics are similar, but the *systems* are not. A Cessna pilot is used to gravity-fed fuel with a "Both" tank selector. A low-wing aircraft requires an electric fuel pump and deliberate tank switching. Fuel mismanagement in an unfamiliar aircraft type consistently appears in NTSB accident reports as the cause — not pilot incompetence, but **negative transfer**: the deeply ingrained habit from one aircraft creating a dangerous error in another. The classic example: a Cessna pilot reaching right to retract flaps on landing rollout in a Bonanza — and instead retracting the landing gear.

**Glass cockpit transitions.** The risk intensifies in Technologically Advanced Aircraft (TAA). Autopilots operate in multiple modes: Heading, NAV, Approach, Vertical Speed, Flight Level Change. A pilot transitioning from steam gauges who doesn't understand what mode the autopilot is in — or worse, assumes it's capturing an altitude when it isn't — is in serious danger. AC 90-109A addresses this directly and recommends treating first flights in a new glass cockpit type as **test flights**: no passengers, no complex airspace, no high-density altitude. Program your GPS *before* you taxi, not on the runway.

**The checkride trap:** Applicants assume BasicMed works fine for any small aircraft. They don't know the seat-removal trick doesn't work, or that international flights require special foreign-country authorization. On unfamiliar aircraft: don't just say "I'd do a checkout." Explain *why* — negative transfer, fuel system differences, automation surprise — and the DPE will know you actually understand it.
